key_findings: The operational context (specifically CPU temperature and core scheduling/frequency) is the primary driver of variation in package-level energy consumption (PKG).
A quadratic relationship exists between CPU temperature and baseline energy consumption, with a negative quadratic coefficient indicating CPU throttling at higher temperatures.
Incorporating execution time (seconds or delta_seconds) into the generalized linear models (GLMs) significantly improves their ability to explain energy variability.

Pinning tasks to specific CPU dies (performance Die 1 or efficiency Die 2 using taskset) does not change the underlying thermodynamic model of the system (verified by negligible Kullback-Leibler divergence).

Pinning workloads to the efficiency cores (Die 2) unexpectedly increases baseline energy consumption, likely because increased runtimes at lower frequencies allow the base package power draw to dominate.
Because execution time is the dominant factor in energy models, performance optimization ('run-to-idle') remains the most viable and effective strategy for metaheuristic energy reduction.
statistical_models: GLM: PKG ~ I(initial_temp^2) + initial_temp * dimension * population_size
GLM: PKG ~ I(initial_temp^2) + initial_temp * dimension * population_size + evaluations
GLM: PKG ~ I(initial_temp^2) + initial_temp * dimension + population_size * evaluations
GLM: PKG ~ initial_temp * dimension * population_size + evaluations * delta_seconds + I(initial_temp^2)
GLM (Time-extended baseline): PKG ~ I(initial_temp^2) + initial_temp * dimension * population_size + seconds
Wilcoxon Rank-Sum Test (wilcox.test): Comparing PKG, seconds, and initial_temp across Base vs. Taskset
Kullback-Leibler Divergence (KL): Quantifying distance between baseline models under different core pinnings

code_chunks.summary: Loads the initial mixed baseline-workload dataset (europar_test.rds) and plots raw package energy (PKG) vs average temperature of the two dies.
code_chunks.relation: Establishes a baseline correlation between temperature and energy consumption, showing distinct trends for baseline and workload runs.

produces.label: fig:europar.initial
produces.caption: Energy spent vs. temperature for the baseline experiment. Workload and baseline runs (base) are represented with different colors, problem dimension is represented with different shapes.

code_chunks.summary: Fits linear and quadratic GLMs on baseline initial temperature and compares them using ANOVA.
code_chunks.relation: Confirms the existence of a negative quadratic temperature term, indicating that system-throttling mitigates energy growth at higher temperatures.

code_chunks.summary: Processes deltas via process_deltas (sandwich subtraction) and fits GLM models predicting PKG energy including quadratic temperature, dimension, population size, evaluations, and delta execution time.
code_chunks.relation: Quantifies the high residual variability (IQR ~68.1) in delta PKG and shows that execution time differences (delta_seconds) and their interaction with evaluations explain the workload variance best.

code_chunks.summary: Plots predicted slopes/predictions of the workload model across initial temperature, population size, and dimension using marginaleffects.
code_chunks.relation: Shows that optimal population size recommendations vary and cross depending on dimension and CPU temperature, indicating that optimal configuration decisions require thermodynamic modeling.

produces.label: fig:europar.initial.model.slopes
produces.caption: Slopes of the model for the workload runs.

code_chunks.summary: Fits a GLM baseline model including the execution time (seconds) variable and compares it to the model without time using ANOVA.
code_chunks.relation: Proves that execution time is highly significant, showing that core-frequency and scheduler decisions are critical context components driving energy.

code_chunks.summary: Loads taskset die 1 dataset (europar_taskset.rds), plots PKG vs. temperature, fits GLMs, and plots baseline PKG vs. seconds colored by temperature.
code_chunks.relation: Evaluates the effect of pinning tasks to performance cores (die 1). Demonstrates that execution time becomes the dominant predictor over temperature under this setting.

produces.label: fig:europar.taskset
produces.caption: Workload energy consumption for the experiment with taskset on die 1; (left) vs. (average) T, (right) vs. time

code_chunks.summary: Combines baseline datasets and computes Kullback-Leibler divergence between predictions of baseline models with and without taskset.
code_chunks.relation: Shows that model distributions are essentially identical, proving that core pinning changes operational parameters but not the underlying thermodynamic relationship.

code_chunks.summary: Performs Wilcoxon rank-sum tests to compare PKG energy, seconds, and initial temperature between Base and Taskset Die 1 setups.
code_chunks.relation: Indicates no significant difference, suggesting the OS naturally schedules the single-threaded task to Die 1 cores when unpinned.

code_chunks.summary: Loads taskset die 2 dataset (europar_taskset_die2.rds), plots PKG vs. temperature, fits GLMs, calculates KL divergence, processes deltas, and plots delta PKG vs. delta seconds.
code_chunks.relation: Evaluates pinning to efficiency cores (die 2). Shows stable model structure (low KL divergence) but shifted physical ranges, indicating that efficiency core runs have a distinct operational context.

produces.label: fig:europar.die2
produces.caption: Energy consumption vs. T for the workload (left), and workload-only energy consumption (Delta PKG) vs. Delta R (right), with color representing problem dimension, taskset on die 2.

code_chunks.summary: Computes summary statistics (means, trimmed means, IQR) for energy, time, and temperature comparing Die 1 and Die 2 baseline runs, and performs Wilcoxon tests.
code_chunks.relation: Provides the mathematical basis showing that baseline energy is slightly higher on Die 2, despite efficiency core designation, because of temperature-driven base power.

code_chunks.summary: Groups processed delta PKG data by dimension, population size, and experiment (Die 2 vs No Die), generating a comparison table.
code_chunks.relation: Demonstrates that Die 2 workloads consume more energy, and pinning fails to reduce measurement uncertainty (IQR remains ~67.5).

produces.label: tab:europar.die2.workload.table
produces.caption: Summary statistics for workload-only (delta) PKG energy for the workload experiment with and without taskset on die 2.

code_chunks.summary: Fits GLM predicting workload energy deltas on die 2 using initial temperature, dimension, population size, evaluations, and delta seconds.
code_chunks.relation: Reveals that initial temperature and delta seconds explain 99.49% of the variance, leaving virtually no room to measure the impact of algorithmic configuration changes.
